One nation will rise against another, and one kingdom against another. There will be earthquakes in many places, and famines. These things are just the beginning of the labor pains.
“As for you, be on your guard. They will hand you over to councils,{b} and you will be flogged in synagogues; you will stand before governors and kings on my account, to bear witness to them.
And first the good news must be proclaimed among all the nations.
Whenever they arrest you and bring you to trial, do not fret beforehand about what you will say; just say whatever is given you at that moment, for it is not you who speak but the Holy Spirit.
Brothers will betray brothers to death, and fathers their children; children will rise against parents and have them put to death.
Everyone will hate you because of my name. But whoever holds out to the end will be saved.
“When you see the desolating abomination{c} standing where he ought not to be—let the reader take note—then those in Judea must escape to the hills.
Anyone on the rooftop must not go down or go inside to fetch anything out of the house;
anyone out in the field must not turn back to pick up a cloak.
How hard it will be in those days for women expecting a child and for mothers with babies at the breast!
Pray that it does not happen in winter.
For those days will bring distress such as has never been from the beginning of the creation God made until now, and never will be again.
Had the Lord not cut short those days, no living being would survive; but for the sake of the chosen, whom he has chosen for himself, he has cut the days short.
And at that time, if anyone says to you, ‘Look, the Messiah is here!’ or ‘Look, he is there!’ do not believe it.
For pretended messiahs and pretended prophets will arise and work signs and marvels, aiming to deceive even the chosen, were that possible.
So keep watch; I have forewarned you of everything.

the stars will be falling out of the sky,
and the powers in the heavens will be shaken.’{d}
Then they will see the Son of Man coming in clouds{e} with great power and glory.
And then he will send out the angels and gather [his] chosen ones from the four winds, from the farthest edge of the earth to the farthest edge of the sky.
“Learn the lesson from the fig tree. As soon as its branch turns tender and puts out leaves, you know summer is close.
So it is with you: when you see these things taking place, know that he{f} is near, right at the doors.
Amen, I tell you, this generation will not pass away before all these things have happened.
Sky and earth will pass away, but my words will never pass away.
“But that day or hour nobody knows—not the angels in heaven, nor the Son,{g} but only the Father.
Be on the lookout and keep alert, since the appointed moment is unknown to you.{h}
It is like a man away on a journey, who leaves his house and puts his slaves in charge, each with his own task, and orders the doorkeeper to keep awake.
Stay awake, then, because the master of the house may return at any time unknown to you—late in the evening, at midnight, at cockcrow, or early in the morning.{i}
Otherwise he may come without warning and find you sleeping.
What I say to you I say to everyone: Keep awake!”

notes.text: I am he: literally “I am,” perhaps echoing the divine self-designation (Exod 3:14; Isa 43:10).
Councils: Greek *synedria*, local Jewish courts.
Desolating abomination: literally “the abomination of desolation,” Dan 9:27; 11:31; 12:11; compare 1 Macc 1:54. The participle “standing” is masculine, suggesting a person.
Isa 13:10; 34:4; compare Joel 2:10.
Coming in clouds: Dan 7:13.
He: or “it.”
Nor the Son: these words, present in all the major manuscripts of Mark, are omitted in some late manuscripts of Matt 24:36.

The appointed moment is unknown to you: literally “you do not know when the time is”; Westcott–Hort bracket “is” (*estin*). Many manuscripts add “and pray” after “keep alert” (Sinaiticus and others); Vaticanus and Bezae lack it.
Late in the evening … early in the morning: the four Roman watches of the night, roughly six to nine in the evening, nine to midnight, midnight to three, and three to six in the morning.

verses.text: Two days remained until the Passover and the feast of Unleavened Bread.{a} Meanwhile the chief priests and scribes were seeking a way to seize Jesus by a trick and put him to death.
For they said, “Not at the feast, in case there is an uproar among the people.”

He was at Bethany in the house of Simon the leper,{b} sitting at the table, when a woman arrived with an alabaster jar of very expensive perfume, pure nard.{c} She broke the jar open and poured the perfume on his head.
Some of those present grumbled indignantly to one another, “What was the point of squandering the ointment like this?
It could have been sold for over three hundred days’ wages{d} and the money given to the poor.” And they spoke sharply to her.
But Jesus said, “Leave her alone. Why are you making trouble for her? She has done a beautiful thing for me.
The poor you always have among you, and you can do good to them [always] whenever you wish; but me you will not always have.
She has done what lay in her power: she has anointed my body ahead of time for its burial.
Amen, I tell you, in every part of the world where the good news is preached, her deed too will be spoken of, so that she is remembered.”
Judas Iscariot,{e} who was one of the Twelve, went to the chief priests in order to hand Jesus over to them.
They were delighted to hear it and promised to pay him in silver. So he kept looking for a convenient opportunity to hand him over.

On the first day of the Unleavened Bread, the day the Passover lambs were slaughtered, his disciples said to him, “Where would you like us to go and get things ready for you to eat the Passover meal?”
He sent two of his disciples with these instructions: “Go into the city, and a man carrying a clay jar of water will meet you. Follow him,
and whatever house he enters, tell its master, ‘The Teacher says: Where is the room set aside for me, so that I can eat the Passover there with my disciples?’
He himself will point out to you a spacious room upstairs, already furnished with couches. Get things ready for us there.”
The disciples set out, came into the city, and found everything just as he had told them; and they prepared the Passover.
When evening came, he arrived with the Twelve.
And as they reclined at the meal, Jesus said, “Amen, I tell you, one of you will betray me—one who is eating with me.”{f}
Grief came over them, and one after another they began asking him, “Surely not I?”
He told them, “It is one of the Twelve, one who is dipping his bread with me into the [one] bowl.
The Son of Man will go as the Scriptures say about him; but how terrible for the one by whom the Son of Man is handed over! It would have been better for that man never to have been born.”
While they were eating, he took a loaf, said the blessing, broke it, and gave it to them with the words, “Take it; this is my body.”{g}
Then he took a cup, gave thanks, and handed it to them, and they all drank from it.
And he told them, “This is my blood of the covenant,{h} poured out on behalf of many.
Amen, I tell you, never again will I drink of the fruit of the vine until that day when I drink it new in God’s kingdom.”
After singing the hymn,{i} they went out to the Mount of Olives.
But once I am raised, I will lead the way before you into Galilee.”
Peter declared, “Everyone else may fall away, but not I.”
Jesus said to him, “Amen, I tell you: this very night, before a rooster crows twice, you will deny me three times.”
But Peter kept protesting all the more forcefully, “Even if it means dying alongside you, I will not disown you!” And all of them were saying the same.
They went to a place named Gethsemane,{k} and he said to his disciples, “Stay here while I pray.”
Taking with him Peter, James, and John, he began to be filled with alarm and anguish.
“My soul is crushed with grief, even to death,”{l} he told them. “Wait here and stay awake.”
Going on a little farther, he fell to the ground and prayed that, if it were possible, the hour might pass him by.
“Abba,{m} Father,” he said, “for you all things are possible. Take this cup away from me. Yet let it be not what I want, but what you want.”
He came back and found them asleep. “Simon,” he said to Peter, “are you sleeping? Had you not the strength to stay awake a single hour?
Keep awake and pray, so that you do not come into the time of testing.{n} The spirit is eager, but human nature is frail.”
Once more he went away and prayed, [saying the same words.]
And again he came and found them sleeping, for their eyes were weighed down; and they had no idea what to say to him.
Coming back a third time, he said to them, “Still asleep? Still taking your rest?{o} It is enough; the hour is here. See, the Son of Man is being betrayed into sinners’ hands.
Get up, let us go. Look, the one betraying me is close at hand.”
And just then, as he was speaking, up came Judas, one of the Twelve, with a mob carrying swords and cudgels, dispatched by the chief priests, scribes, and elders.
His betrayer had given them a prearranged sign: “The man I kiss—he is the one. Take hold of him and lead him off securely.”
As soon as he arrived, he went straight up to Jesus, said, “Rabbi!” and kissed him warmly.
Then they laid hands on him and arrested him.
One of those standing nearby drew a sword and slashed at the high priest’s slave, slicing off his ear.
Jesus responded, “Have you come out with swords and cudgels to capture me as though I were a bandit?
Every day I was among you in the temple teaching, and you never arrested me. But this is happening so that the Scriptures will be fulfilled.”
Then they all deserted him and ran away.
A young man was following him, wearing only a linen cloth over his naked body. They seized him,
but he left the linen cloth behind and fled naked.{p}
They took Jesus away to the high priest,{q} and all the chief priests, elders, and scribes assembled.
Peter trailed behind at a distance, as far as the inside of the high priest’s courtyard, and he was sitting among the attendants, keeping warm by the blaze.
Meanwhile the chief priests and the entire Council{r} kept searching for evidence against Jesus that would justify putting him to death, yet they could find none.
Many gave false evidence against him, but their statements did not agree.
Some men then rose and testified falsely against him, saying,
“We ourselves heard him say, ‘I will pull down this temple made with hands, and within three days I will build another, not made with hands.’ ”
But even so, their accounts were inconsistent.
Then the high priest stood up in their midst and questioned Jesus: “Have you no answer to make? What is this testimony these men bring against you?”
He kept silent and said nothing in reply. Once more the high priest put a question to him: “Are you the Christ, the Son of the Blessed?”{s}
“I am,” said Jesus, “and you will see the Son of Man seated at the right hand of the Power{t} and coming with the clouds of heaven.”{u}
At that the high priest ripped his garments. “What further need have we of witnesses?” he said.
“You heard him blaspheme. How does it seem to you?” And all of them judged him worthy of death.
Then some started spitting at him; they covered his face, punched him, and taunted him, “Prophesy!” And the attendants took him and slapped him.
Peter was down in the courtyard when one of the high priest’s maidservants came along.
Noticing Peter warming himself, she looked closely at him and said, “You too were with the Nazarene, this Jesus.”
But he denied it: “I have no idea what you mean—I don’t understand it.” And he went outside into the entryway.{v}
The servant girl saw him there and began telling the bystanders once more, “This fellow is one of them.”
Again he denied it. A little while afterward the bystanders said to Peter again, “You certainly are one of them, for you are a Galilean.”{w}
Then he began to put himself under a curse and to swear, “I have no knowledge of this man you speak of.”

And right then the rooster crowed for the second time, and Peter recalled the word Jesus had spoken to him: “Twice the rooster will crow, and before that you will have disowned me three times.” And he broke down and wept.{x}

notes.text: Passover … Unleavened Bread: the Passover meal on the evening beginning 15 Nisan, followed by the seven-day festival of Unleavened Bread (Exod 12:1–20; Lev 23:5–8).
Simon the leper: presumably a man Jesus had healed. *Simon* means “he has heard.”
Pure nard: Greek *nardou pistikēs*, spikenard, an aromatic oil imported from the Himalayas; *pistikēs* probably means “genuine.”
More than three hundred days’ wages: literally “more than three hundred denarii,” a denarius being a laborer’s day’s wage.
Iscariot: probably Hebrew *ish Qeriyot*, “man of Kerioth,” a town in Judea (Josh 15:25).
Eating with me: compare Ps 41:9.
This is my body: Westcott–Hort and the earliest manuscripts lack “eat” after “take it,” which many later manuscripts add (compare Matt 26:26).
Blood of the covenant: Exod 24:8; compare Zech 9:11. Many manuscripts read “the new covenant” (compare Luke 22:20; 1 Cor 11:25); Westcott–Hort, following Sinaiticus and Vaticanus, lack “new.”
The hymn: probably the second half of the Hallel (Pss 115–118), sung at the close of the Passover meal.
Zech 13:7.
Gethsemane: Aramaic *gat shemanim*, “oil press.”
Abba: Aramaic for “father,” the intimate address of a child to a parent; compare Rom 8:15; Gal 4:6.
Time of testing: or “temptation.”

Still asleep? Still taking your rest?: or, as a command, “Sleep on now and take your rest.” *It is enough*: Greek *apechei*, of uncertain meaning; perhaps “the account is settled,” “he (the betrayer) has received payment,” or “it is far off.” Bezae and some others add “the end.”
Fled naked: this episode is found only in Mark. Some have suggested the young man was Mark himself, but this is conjecture.
The high priest: Caiaphas (Matt 26:57), high priest AD 18–36.
Council: Greek *synedrion*, the Sanhedrin, the supreme Jewish court in Jerusalem, presided over by the high priest.
The Blessed: a reverent Jewish substitute for the name of God.
The Power: another reverent substitute for the name of God. The words echo Ps 110:1.
Entryway: or “forecourt.” Many manuscripts add “and a rooster crowed” (Alexandrinus, Bezae and others); Westcott–Hort, with Sinaiticus and Vaticanus, lack it.
Galilean: many later manuscripts add “and your speech gives you away” (compare Matt 26:73).
He broke down and wept: the meaning of the Greek *epibalōn* is uncertain; perhaps “he thought of it,” “he threw himself down,” or “he covered his head.”

verses.text: Early in the morning, the chief priests conferred with the elders, the scribes and the entire Council. Then they tied up Jesus, took him away, and handed him over to Pilate.{a}
Pilate questioned him: “You are the king of the Jews?” “You say so,”{b} he answered.
The chief priests kept bringing many charges against him.
So Pilate questioned him once more: “Have you nothing to say in reply? Listen to how many accusations they are making against you!”
But Jesus gave no further answer at all, which left Pilate astonished.
At each festival Pilate used to set free for them one prisoner, whomever they requested.
There was a man called Barabbas{c} held in prison with the rebels who had committed murder during the uprising.
So the crowd went up and started demanding that he follow his usual practice for them.
Pilate replied, “Is it your wish that I set free the king of the Jews for you?”
For he was aware that it was out of envy that the chief priests had handed Jesus over.
The chief priests, however, incited the crowd to ask that he free Barabbas for them in place of Jesus.
Pilate spoke to them again: “Then what am I to do with the one you call the king of the Jews?”
They shouted back, “Crucify him!”
“Why? What crime has he committed?” Pilate asked. But they only shouted louder, “Crucify him!”
Pilate, intent on pleasing the crowd, released Barabbas to them; and he had Jesus scourged{d} and then gave him up for crucifixion.
The soldiers marched him off inside the palace courtyard (the governor’s residence){e} and summoned the whole company of troops.{f}
They dressed him in purple, twisted together a crown of thorns, and set it on his head.
Then they began to salute him: “Hail, king of the Jews!”
They kept hitting him on the head with a reed and spitting on him, and bending their knees, they paid him mock homage.
When their mockery was over, they pulled the purple robe off him, dressed him in his own garments, and took him out for crucifixion.
A passerby, Simon of Cyrene,{g} the father of Alexander and Rufus,{h} was coming in from the country, and they forced him to carry Jesus’ cross.
They brought Jesus to the place called Golgotha, which translated means “Place of a Skull.”{i}
They held out to him wine laced with myrrh,{j} but he would not take it.
And they crucified him and divided up his clothes, throwing dice for them to see what each would take.{k}
It was nine o’clock in the morning{l} when they crucified him.
The notice of the charge against him was inscribed: THE KING OF THE JEWS.
Two bandits{m} were crucified along with him, the one at his right, the other at his left.
People going by hurled insults at him, shaking their heads{o} and saying, “Ha! You who would tear down the temple and rebuild it in three days,
save yourself and come down from the cross!”
In the same way the chief priests, along with the scribes, mocked him among themselves: “He saved others, but he cannot save himself!
This Messiah, this king of Israel—let him climb down from the cross this minute, so we can see it and believe!” Even the men crucified beside him reviled him.
When noon came, darkness fell over the whole land{p} until three in the afternoon.{q}
At three o’clock Jesus cried out in a loud voice, “Eloi, Eloi, lema sabachthani?”{r} which translated means, “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?”
Some of the bystanders who heard it said, “Listen, he is calling Elijah.”
Someone ran and filled a sponge with sour wine,{s} fixed it to a reed, and held it up for him to drink, saying, “Leave him alone! Let us see if Elijah comes to take him down.”
Then Jesus gave a great cry and breathed out his life.
And the curtain of the temple{t} was torn in two from top to bottom.
When the centurion{u} who stood facing him saw that he had died in this way,{v} he said, “Truly this man was God’s Son!”{w}
Some women were also looking on from far away, among them Mary Magdalene,{x} Mary the mother of James the younger and of Joses, and Salome.{y}
While he was in Galilee they used to follow him and provide for him; and many other women were there as well, who had traveled up to Jerusalem with him.
It was already evening, and because it was Preparation Day—the day before a Sabbath—
Joseph of Arimathea{z} came, a prominent Council member who was also looking for God’s kingdom. He ventured boldly into Pilate’s presence and requested Jesus’ body.
Pilate was astonished that he had already died. He called the centurion and asked whether Jesus had been dead for long.{aa}
Once the centurion had confirmed it, Pilate gave Joseph the body.
Joseph bought a linen cloth, took Jesus down, wrapped him in it, and laid him in a tomb that had been cut into the rock. He then rolled a stone across the tomb’s entrance.
Mary Magdalene and Mary the mother of Joses saw the place where they put him.

notes.text: Pilate: Pontius Pilate, Roman prefect (governor) of Judea AD 26–36.
You say so: an evasive or affirmative answer, meaning “That is your word for it” or “It is as you say.”
Barabbas: Aramaic *bar Abba*, “son of the father.” Some manuscripts of Matthew (27:16–17) give his name as “Jesus Barabbas.”
Scourged: Greek *phragellōsas*, from Latin *flagellum*, a scourge of leather thongs weighted with bone or metal, the brutal preliminary to crucifixion.
Governor’s residence: Greek *praitōrion* (Latin *praetorium*), the official residence of the Roman governor in Jerusalem.
Whole company of troops: literally “the whole cohort,” Greek *speira*, a unit of a Roman legion, nominally 600 soldiers, though the term was used of smaller detachments.
Cyrene: a Greek city on the coast of North Africa (modern Libya), with a large Jewish community. *Simon* means “he has heard.”
Alexander and Rufus: *Alexander* is Greek, “defender of men”; *Rufus* is Latin, “red.” They were apparently known to Mark’s readers (compare Rom 16:13).
Golgotha: Aramaic *gulgulta*, “skull.” The Latin equivalent, *calvaria*, gives the traditional name “Calvary.”
Wine laced with myrrh: a drink perhaps meant to dull the pain (compare Prov 31:6).
Ps 22:18. *Throwing dice*: literally “casting lots.”
Nine in the morning: literally “the third hour,” counting from sunrise at about six o’clock.
Bandits: or “rebels” (Greek *lēstai*), the term Josephus uses for insurgents.

Verse 28 is lacking in the Westcott–Hort text and in the earliest manuscripts (Sinaiticus, Vaticanus, Alexandrinus, Bezae and others). Many later manuscripts add, “And the scripture was fulfilled that says, ‘He was counted among the lawless’ ” (Isa 53:12; compare Luke 22:37).
Shaking their heads: compare Ps 22:7; 109:25; Lam 2:15.
Land: or “earth.” Compare Amos 8:9.
Noon … three in the afternoon: literally “the sixth hour … the ninth hour.”

Eloi, Eloi, lema sabachthani: Ps 22:1, in Aramaic, transliterated in Greek. *Eloi* is Aramaic for “my God” (the Westcott–Hort reading here); some manuscripts have the Hebrew form *Eli* (compare Matt 27:46). *Three o’clock*: literally “the ninth hour.” Westcott–Hort bracket the second “my God” in Mark’s translation.
Sour wine: Greek *oxos*, a cheap wine vinegar drunk by soldiers and laborers. Compare Ps 69:21.
Curtain of the temple: probably the curtain separating the Most Holy Place from the Holy Place (Exod 26:31–33).
Centurion: a Roman officer commanding about a hundred soldiers.
Died in this way: literally “breathed out thus.” Many manuscripts read “cried out and breathed his last in this way.”
God’s Son: or “a son of God.” The Greek lacks the article; the phrase may express a Roman soldier’s recognition of a divine man or the full Christian confession (compare 1:1, 11; 9:7).
Mary Magdalene: that is, Mary of Magdala, a town on the western shore of the lake; *Magdala* comes from Aramaic *migdal*, “tower.”
Salome: from Hebrew *shalom*, “peace.” She may be the mother of James and John (compare Matt 27:56).
Arimathea: probably Ramathaim (Ramah), the birthplace of Samuel (1 Sam 1:1), northwest of Jerusalem; the name means “heights.” *Joseph* means “may he add” (Gen 30:24).
Had been dead for some time: Vaticanus, Bezae and some others, followed by Westcott–Hort in the margin, read “was already dead.”

verses.text: Once the Sabbath had ended, Mary Magdalene, Mary the mother of James, and Salome purchased fragrant spices, intending to go and anoint him.
Very early on the first day of the week, just after sunrise, they made their way to the tomb.
They were saying to one another, “Who is going to roll the stone back from the tomb’s entrance for us?”
But when they looked up, they saw that the stone—an exceedingly large one—had already been rolled away.
Going into the tomb, they saw a young man dressed in a white robe sitting on the right-hand side, and they were struck with amazement.
“Do not be so amazed,” he said to them. “You are looking for Jesus the Nazarene, the one who was crucified. He has been raised; he is not here. See the spot where they laid him.
Now go and tell his disciples, and Peter, ‘He is going on ahead of you into Galilee. There you will see him, just as he told you.’ ”
They came out and fled from the tomb, seized with trembling and bewilderment; and they said nothing to anyone, for they were afraid.{a}
[[After he rose early on the first day of the week, he appeared first to Mary Magdalene, from whom he had driven out seven demons.
She went and told those who had been with him, as they mourned and wept.
But when they heard that he was alive and that she had seen him, they would not believe it.
After this he showed himself in another form to two of them as they were walking along on their way into the country.
They went back and told the others, but these did not believe them either.

Later he showed himself to the eleven themselves as they reclined at table, and he rebuked them for their unbelief and stubbornness of heart, because they had not believed those who had seen him after he was raised.{b}
He said to them, “Go out into all the world and announce the good news to the whole creation.
Whoever believes and is baptized will be saved, but whoever refuses to believe will be condemned.
Those who believe will be attended by these signs: they will cast out demons by my name; they will speak in new tongues;{c}
they will pick up snakes [with their hands],{d} and if they drink any deadly poison it will do them no harm; they will lay their hands on the sick, and these will recover.”
So then, after speaking with them, the Lord [Jesus] was taken up into heaven and sat down at God’s right hand.{e}
Then the disciples set out and proclaimed the message far and wide, the Lord working alongside them and confirming the word through the accompanying signs.]]{f}

notes.text: For they were afraid: here the earliest manuscripts, Sinaiticus and Vaticanus, end the Gospel of Mark, as do the Sinaitic Syriac, about a hundred Armenian manuscripts, and the two oldest Georgian manuscripts; Eusebius and Jerome report that almost all Greek copies known to them ended here. Westcott–Hort print 16:9–20 and the shorter ending within double brackets as early additions, not part of Mark’s original text. Whether Mark intended to end at 16:8, or a lost ending once followed, remains debated. See the note at 16:20 for the endings found in other manuscripts.
Raised: Westcott–Hort bracket “from the dead.”
New tongues: Vaticanus lacks “new”; Westcott–Hort retain it.
With their hands: Westcott–Hort bracket these words, which Alexandrinus and many others lack.
God’s right hand: compare Ps 110:1. *Jesus* is bracketed by Westcott–Hort.

The endings of Mark. (1) The *longer ending* (16:9–20, printed here in double brackets) appears in Alexandrinus, Ephraemi, Bezae, Washingtonianus and the great majority of later manuscripts, and Irenaeus (late 2nd century) knew of it. Its vocabulary and style differ markedly from the rest of Mark, and it draws on the resurrection accounts of the other Gospels and Acts. (2) The *shorter ending*, which Westcott–Hort also print in double brackets, comes after 16:8 in a few manuscripts (alone in Codex Bobiensis and the Old Latin k; in several Greek manuscripts it is followed by the longer ending). In summary, it says the women briefly passed on their instructions to Peter’s companions, and that afterward Jesus himself sent out through them, from east to west, the holy and unfading message of eternal salvation. [Amen.] (3) The *Freer Logion*, found only in Codex Washingtonianus (W, 4th–5th century) after 16:14, includes in part a reply from the disciples that this age of lawlessness and unbelief lies under Satan, who prevents God’s truth and power from overcoming the unclean powers of the spirits, and so they ask Christ to reveal his righteousness at once. Christ answers that the span of years of Satan’s authority is complete, but that other terrible things are near, even for those sinners for whom he was handed over to death, so that they might turn to the truth, sin no more, and inherit the spiritual and imperishable glory of righteousness in heaven. Jerome mentions a form of this saying (*Against the Pelagians* 2.15). None of the early papyri of Mark (P45, P88, P137) preserves this chapter.
